dissents.topic: Severity of the missing specification/contract for the @layer exception

positions.position: P1 — the spec rule ('@layer statement form is permitted before @import per CSS Cascade Level 5') is encoded only in a boolean expression; without a comment naming the spec, substitutability cannot be verified against the standard.
P1 — the predicate is UNREASONED: the precondition, AST invariant, and intent are nowhere stated; correctness rests on tests rather than a stated argument.
P2 — flags the same missing literate comment but treats it as a stylistic readability improvement, not a blocker.
P2 — same observation framed as complecting / naming the concept; readability and future-proofing nit, not a blocker.
P2 — same observation, framed as a cosmetic readability nit; ship-as-is is acceptable.
Not flagged — predicate 'reads fine'; no comment or named helper requested.

dissents.topic: Whether `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'` is acceptable as written

positions.position: P1-adjacent — the predicate happens to coincide with intent but the AST invariant is never stated; demands `node.nodes !== undefined` written directly plus a comment stating the PostCSS invariant.
P2 — leaks PostCSS AST representation; wants it encapsulated behind a named helper like `hasBlock(node)`.
P2 — easy but not simple; ties the rule to PostCSS's internal representation; name the concept once.
P2 — wordier and asymmetric; prefers `!node.nodes` or `node.nodes == null`. Minor readability nit.
P2 — verbose; prefers `node.nodes == null` or `node.nodes !== undefined`. Not a blocker.
P2 — more ceremony than needed; prefers `node.nodes === undefined` or `!node.nodes`.

dissents.topic: What additional test cases are needed

positions.position: Add the positive symmetric case: bare `@layer foo;` before `@import` should remain accepted, to pin the predicate from both sides.
Add an accept case for statement-form `@layer foo, bar;` followed by `@import` to lock in both halves of the contract.
Add both `@layer foo, bar;` (statement-list, allowed) and a non-empty `@layer foo { .a {} }` (block with content, rejected).
Add non-empty layer block and a statement-form layer before @import to pin the data-shape distinction.
Add a non-empty block case (`@layer foo { .x {} }`) for completeness; minor.

Add tests for `@layer foo, bar;` (bodyless, multiple names), `@layer {}` (anonymous block), nested layer blocks, and plugin-produced layer at-rules — but notes tests alone cannot prove absence of bugs.

issues.description: Contract for the @layer exception is implicit; the CSS spec rule justifying it is not written down in code or comment
issues.detail: The original code stated 'layer is allowed before @import' as a flat exception. The fix correctly narrows it to 'layer without a block is allowed' — matching CSS Cascade Level 5 semantics where statement-form `@layer foo, bar;` is a forward declaration permitted before `@import` while block-form `@layer foo {}` is a definition that is not. But the spec rule that justifies the exception is encoded only in a negated boolean expression. A comment naming the invariant (and linking the relevant CSS spec section) would let the next maintainer verify substitutability against the standard rather than reverse-engineering it from the negation.

issues.description: Predicate `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'` encodes intent as a property check on a PostCSS-internal field without stating the AST invariant it relies on
issues.detail: The author wishes to distinguish a layer at-rule with a block from one without. The chosen test is a property check on PostCSS's internal `nodes` field — `@layer foo;` arrives with `nodes` undefined while `@layer foo {}` arrives with `nodes` defined as `[]`. The predicate happens to coincide with intent for the inputs tested but the precondition ('a PostCSS at-rule has a block iff its `nodes` field is not undefined') is never stated. Dijkstra flags this as folklore-as-substitute-for-reasoning and demands the invariant be written down; the milder reviewers agree the discriminator leaks the PostCSS representation through what should be a named predicate like `hasBlock(node)`.

issues.description: Negated compound predicate `!(nodeName === 'layer' && typeof node.nodes === 'undefined')` is harder to scan than the surrounding parallel equality checks
issues.detail: The new condition inserts a negated conjunction into an already long six-clause boolean guard (isAtRule, four name comparisons, optionsMatches, isStandardSyntaxAtRule). Multiple reviewers recommend extracting a small named predicate — `isLayerStatement(node)`, `hasBlock(node)`, or `isDisallowedPrecedingNode(node)` — so the main expression keeps its parallel `nodeName !== X` shape and the intent is self-evident at the call site. Dijkstra additionally wants the precondition and postcondition of the extracted predicate stated in prose above the function.

issues.description: Prefer direct equality (`node.nodes === undefined`, `!node.nodes`, or `node.nodes == null`) over `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'`
issues.detail: PostCSS at-rules either have a `.nodes` array or do not; the `typeof === 'undefined'` form is verbose, asymmetric with how the rest of the file inspects nodes, and matches no idiom used nearby. A direct equality reads the same, is shorter, and (in the `== null` form) also handles the theoretical `null` case. Stylistic only, not a correctness issue.

issues.description: Test coverage misses the positive symmetric accept case for statement-form `@layer` before `@import`
issues.detail: The diff adds the reject case `@layer foo {}` before `@import`, which pins the new behavior. The contract has two halves — block-form rejects, statement-form accepts — and only the reject half is exercised in this diff. A complementary accept test for `@layer foo, bar;` followed by `@import url(...)` would lock in both sides of the substitution boundary and prevent a future change from accidentally collapsing both forms back to either 'always reject' or 'always accept'. May already exist in the test file; worth verifying.

issues.description: Test coverage misses the non-empty layer-block case
issues.detail: The added test uses `@layer foo {}` — an empty block. The fix keys off `node.nodes` being defined, which is also true for non-empty blocks, so a test like `@layer foo { .x {} }` exercises the same path but documents intent and guards against a future refactor that distinguishes empty vs non-empty `nodes` arrays (e.g. checking `.length === 0` instead of presence).

issues.description: Test coverage misses edge-case layer forms: anonymous block `@layer {}`, nested layer blocks, and plugin-produced layer at-rules
issues.detail: Dijkstra notes that one added test demonstrates the prior bug but does not demonstrate the absence of further ones. Anonymous block-form (`@layer {}`), nested layer blocks, and layer at-rules produced by syntax-extension plugins whose `nodes` property may differ are all untested. The current predicate's behavior on these inputs is asserted only by AST-shape folklore, not by tests or a stated invariant.

synthesis.summary: All six reviewers agree the patch is small, behaviorally correct, and ships with a test and changeset: it correctly distinguishes statement-form `@layer foo;` (permitted before `@import` per CSS Cascade Level 5) from block-form `@layer foo {}` (not permitted) by inspecting whether the PostCSS node has a `.nodes` array. The panel's strongest shared claims are stylistic and contract-hygiene: the negated compound predicate would read better as a named helper (`isLayerStatement` / `hasBlock`), `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'` should be a direct equality check, and test coverage should pin both halves of the contract (statement-form accept case) plus a non-empty-block case. The strongest preserved disagreement is severity of the missing specification: Liskov and Dijkstra treat the unstated CSS spec rule and unstated PostCSS AST invariant as P1 contract/reasoning defects that should block merge until written down, while Knuth, Hickey, Pike, and Torvalds treat the same observations as P2 readability nits — Torvalds explicitly says the predicate 'reads fine' and recommends ACCEPT as-is. A secondary split is over how exhaustively the test set must cover layer-form edge cases, with Dijkstra alone calling for anonymous blocks, nested layer blocks, and plugin-produced layer nodes.
